en: Slightly acidic rainwater slowly dissolved the underground limestone rocks over millions of years to carve the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River.
Heat from underground magma boils groundwater into steam, which then spins turbines to generate electricity at the Tiwi geothermal plant.
Stone walls on the Banaue Rice Terraces trap rainwater and hold soil in place, preventing erosion on steep mountain slopes.
The southwest monsoon picks up moisture while crossing the West Philippine Sea, causing heavy rainfall when it hits Luzon.
Warm Pacific ocean water evaporates and rises rapidly, creating the low-pressure spinning storms we call typhoons.
Thick, sticky lava from Mayon Volcano cools quickly and piles up near the vent, building its perfect cone shape.
Water from Lake Lanao flows down steep mountains through the Agus River, spinning turbines to generate hydroelectric power for Mindanao.
Unusually warm ocean temperatures stress coral polyps in the Tubbataha Reefs, causing them to expel colorful algae and turn white.
Rainwater slowly eroded the soft limestone in Bohol, leaving behind the harder rock formations that form the Chocolate Hills.
When hot magma touches the cold water of Taal Lake, it instantly flashes into steam, causing explosive volcanic eruptions.
The warm Kuroshio Ocean Current flows past the eastern Philippines, bringing nutrient-rich waters that support large populations of marine fish.
Dense mangrove roots in Olango Island trap moving sand and slow ocean waves, protecting the coastline from severe erosion.
